claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Slack and Hatch, 1967 and Langdale, 2011.

claims.claim: The morphology of C4 leaves is typically modified into Kranz anatomy that consists of repeating units of vein, bundle sheath (BS) and mesophyll (M) cells.
claims.source: The morphology of C4 leaves is typically modified into so-called Kranz anatomy that consists of repeating units of vein, bundle sheath (BS) and mesophyll (M) cells (Hattersley, 1984; Langdale, 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hattersley, 1984 and Langdale, 2011, and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In C4 plants, photosynthetic metabolism becomes modified and compartmentalised between the M and BS, with M cells lacking RuBisCO but containing high activities of PEPC.
claims.source: Photosynthetic metabolism becomes modified and compartmentalised between the M and BS, with M cells lacking RuBisCO but instead containing high activities of the alternate carboxylase PEPC to generate C4 acids.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about C4 photosynthesis supported by the general literature.

claims.claim: C4 acids are decarboxylated by at least one of three enzymes within BS cells: NADP-ME, NAD-ME, or PCK.
claims.source: C4 acids are decarboxylated by at least one of three enzymes within BS cells: NADP- or NAD-dependent malic enzymes (NADP-ME or NAD-ME respectively), or phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PCK) (Hatch et al., 1975).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hatch et al., 1975.

claims.claim: Specific lineages of C4 species have typically been classified into one of three sub-types based on the activity of decarboxylases and anatomical and cellular traits.
claims.source: Specific lineages of C4 species have typically been classified into one of three sub-types, based on the activity of these decarboxylases, as well as anatomical and cellular traits that consistently correlate with each other (Furbank, 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Furbank, 2011.

claims.claim: The genetic mechanisms underlying the evolution of cell-specific gene expression in C4 plants involve both alterations to cis-elements and trans-acting factors.
claims.source: The genetic mechanisms underlying the evolution of cell-specific gene expression associated with the separation of photosynthetic metabolism between M and BS cells involve both alterations to cis-elements and trans-acting factors (Akyildiz et al., 2007; Brown et al., 2011; Kajala et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: Phylogenetically independent lineages of C4 plants have co-opted homologous mechanisms to generate cell specificity.
claims.source: Phylogenetically independent lineages of C4 plants have co-opted homologous mechanisms to generate cell specificity (Brown et al., 2011)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2011.

claims.claim: C3–C4 intermediates are species exhibiting characteristics of both C3 or C4 photosynthesis.
claims.source: Clues to this question exist in the form of C3–C4 intermediates, species exhibiting characteristics of both C3 or C4 photosynthesis, such as the activity or localisation of C4 cycle enzymes (Hattersley and Stone, 1986), the possession of one or more anatomical or cellular adaptations associated with C4 photosynthesis (Moore et al., 1987), or combinations of both (e.g., Kennedy et al., 1980; Kotayeva et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies describing C3-C4 intermediates.

claims.claim: Data was consolidated from 43 studies encompassing 18 C3, 18 C4, and 37 C3–C4 intermediate species from 22 genera.
claims.source: To parameterise the phenotypic landscape underlying photosynthetic phenotypes, data was consolidated from 43 studies encompassing 18 C3, 18 C4, and 37 C3–C4 intermediate species from 22 genera (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the data collection methodology used in the study.

claims.claim: The C3–C4 species are from 18 independent lineages likely representing 18 distinct evolutionary origins of C3–C4 intermediacy.
claims.source: These C3–C4 species are from 18 independent lineages likely representing 18 distinct evolutionary origins of C3–C4 intermediacy (Sage et al., 2011a) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sage et al., 2011a and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Principal components analysis confirmed the phenotypic intermediacy of the C3–C4 species.
claims.source: Principal components analysis (PCA) was performed to confirm the phenotypic intermediacy of the C3–C4 species (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the PCA results shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The sister-group relationships of C3–C4 species with congeneric C4 clades support the notion that C3–C4 species represent phenotypic states through which transitions to C4 photosynthesis could occur.
claims.source: This result, the sister-group relationships of C3–C4 species with congeneric C4 clades (McKown et al., 2005; Vogan et al., 2007; Christin et al., 2011a; Sage et al., 2011a; Khoshravesh et al., 2012) and the prevalence of extant C3–C4 species in genera with the most recent origins of C4 photosynthesis (Christin et al., 2011b) all support the notion that C3–C4 species represent phenotypic states through which transitions to C4 photosynthesis could occur.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple phylogenetic studies.

claims.claim: The combined traits of C3–C4 intermediate species represent samples from across the space of phenotypes connecting C3 to C4 photosynthesis.
claims.source: The combined traits of C3–C4 intermediate species therefore represent samples from across the space of phenotypes connecting C3 to C4 photosynthesis (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the phylogenetic relationships and phenotypic data, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Within the meta-analysis data, C3–C4 phenotypes were available for 33 eudicot and 4 monocot species.
claims.source: Within our meta-analysis data, C3–C4 phenotypes were available for 33 eudicot and 4 monocot species.
claims.evidence: This describes the taxonomic composition of the dataset.

claims.claim: 16 and 17 of the C3-C4 species have extant congeneric relatives performing NADP-ME or NAD-ME sub-type C4 photosynthesis respectively.
claims.source: 16 and 17 of these species have extant congeneric relatives performing NADP-ME or NAD-ME sub-type C4 photosynthesis respectively.
claims.evidence: This describes the phylogenetic relationships of the C3-C4 species in the dataset.

claims.claim: No C3–C4 relatives of PCK sub-type C4 species are known.
claims.source: No C3–C4 relatives of PCK sub-type C4 species are known (Sage et al., 2011a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sage et al., 2011a.

claims.claim: The expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm and hierarchical clustering were used to impartially assign binary scores to quantitative traits.
claims.source: For quantitative traits the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm and hierarchical clustering were used to impartially assign binary scores (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used for data processing, illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: A 16-dimensional phenotype space with 65,536 nodes was defined corresponding to all possible combinations of presence and absence scores for each characteristic.
claims.source: This defined a 16-dimensional phenotype space with 216 (65,536) nodes corresponding to all possible combinations of presence (1) and absence (0) scores for each characteristic.
claims.evidence: This describes the mathematical structure of the phenotype space used in the model.

claims.claim: The phenotypic landscape underlying the evolution of C4 photosynthesis was modelled as a transition network with weighted edges describing the probability of transitions between phenotypic states.
claims.source: The phenotypic landscape underlying the evolution of C4 photosynthesis was then modelled as a transition network, with weighted edges describing the probability of transitions occurring between two phenotypic states (two nodes on the hypercube, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study, illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Inferential machinery based on Hidden Markov Models was developed to constrain the structure of phenotypic landscapes using observed intermediate points.
claims.source: To do this, we developed inferential machinery based on the framework of Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) (Rabiner, 1989) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4)
claims.evidence: This describes the novel methodology developed in the study, with citation to the HMM framework.

claims.claim: A Bayesian MCMC procedure was used to sample from the set of networks most compatible with the meta-analysis dataset.
claims.source: A Bayesian MCMC procedure was used to sample from the set of networks most compatible with the meta-analysis dataset, and thus most likely to represent the underlying dynamics of C4 evolution.
claims.evidence: This describes the statistical methodology used in the study.

claims.claim: The model imposed that only one C4 trait may be acquired at a time, and loss of acquired C4 traits was forbidden.
claims.source: To model the evolutionary paths generating C4 without requiring additional dimensionality, we imposed that only one C4 trait may be acquired at a time, and loss of acquired C4 traits was forbidden.
claims.evidence: This describes a constraint of the modeling approach.

claims.claim: The approach clearly assigned equal acquisition probabilities to traits whose timing was linked in the underlying dataset, even when 50% of the data was occluded.
claims.source: Our approach clearly assigned equal acquisition probabilities to traits whose timing was linked in the underlying dataset, even when 50% of the data was occluded (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the positive control test shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The approach is able to detect the simultaneous acquisition of traits in evolution, even though single-trait acquisitions are simulated.
claims.source: These data are consistent with this approach detecting the simultaneous acquisition of traits in evolution, even though single-trait acquisitions are simulated.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the positive control tests.

claims.claim: For 29 occluded traits, 18 were strongly predicted to be present or absent, and of these 18 strongly predicted traits, 15 were correct.
claims.source: For 29 occluded traits 18 were strongly predicted to be present or absent, and the remaining 11 predictions were neutral. Of the 18 strongly predicted traits (i.e., <25% or >75% probability), 15 were correct, with only one false positive and two false negative predictions (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This describes the validation results shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The approach assigns neutral predictions much more frequently than false positive or false negative predictions.
claims.source: The approach therefore assigns neutral predictions much more frequently than false positive or false negative predictions, suggesting that its outputs are highly conservative, and thus unlikely to produce artefacts.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation results.

claims.claim: Quantitative real-time PCR experimentally verified a subset of predictions relating to abundance of C4 enzymes not previously measured.
claims.source: Quantitative real-time PCR experimentally verified a subset of these, relating to abundance of C4 enzymes not previously measured (Figure 2D–E).
claims.evidence: This describes experimental validation shown in Figure 2D-E.

claims.claim: The results are consistent with previous work proposing that BS-specificity of GDC occurs prior to the evolution of C4 metabolism.
claims.source: These results were consistent with previous work on subsets of C4 lineages that proposed the BS-specificity of GDC occurs prior to the evolution of C4 metabolism (Hylton et al., 1988; Rawsthorne et al., 1988; Devi et al., 1995; Sage et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Loss of RuBisCO from M cells occurs late in C4 evolution.
claims.source: These results were consistent with previous work on subsets of C4 lineages that proposed the BS-specificity of GDC occurs prior to the evolution of C4 metabolism (Hylton et al., 1988; Rawsthorne et al., 1988; Devi et al., 1995; Sage et al., 2012), and loss of RuBisCO from M cells occurs late (Cheng et al., 1988; Khoshravesh et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by the model results.

claims.claim: Alterations to leaf anatomy and cell-specificity and increased abundance of multiple C4 cycle enzymes were predicted to evolve prior to any alteration to RuBisCO and PEPC.
claims.source: Alterations to leaf anatomy as well as cell-specificity and increased abundance of multiple C4 cycle enzymes were predicted to evolve prior to any alteration to the primary C3 and C4 photosynthetic enzymes RuBisCO and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the model shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: There was strong evidence for enlargement of BS cells as an early innovation in most C4 lineages.
claims.source: There was also strong evidence for enlargement of BS cells as an early innovation in most C4 lineages (Figure 3), consistent with the suggestion that this was an ancestral state within C3 ancestors of C4 grass lineages and that this contributed to the high number of C4 origins within this family (Christin et al., 2013; Griffiths et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This finding from Figure 3 is consistent with cited studies on grass lineages.

claims.claim: The compartmentation of PEPC into M cells and its increased abundance compared with C3 leaves was predicted to occur at similar times.
claims.source: The compartmentation of PEPC into M cells and its increased abundance compared with C3 leaves was predicted to occur at similar times, but for all other C4 enzymes the evolution of increased abundance and cellular compartmentation were clearly separated by the acquisition of other traits (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: For all C4 enzymes except PEPC, the evolution of increased abundance and cellular compartmentation were clearly separated by the acquisition of other traits.
claims.source: The compartmentation of PEPC into M cells and its increased abundance compared with C3 leaves was predicted to occur at similar times, but for all other C4 enzymes the evolution of increased abundance and cellular compartmentation were clearly separated by the acquisition of other traits (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The result that cell-specificity and increased expression are separated is consistent with molecular analysis showing these are mediated by different cis-elements.
claims.source: This result is consistent with molecular analysis of genes encoding C4 enzymes that indicates cell-specificity and increased expression are mediated by different cis-elements (Akyildiz et al., 2007; Kajala et al., 2012; Wiludda et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to molecular studies.

claims.claim: Repeating the analysis using scores assigned by hierarchical clustering did not affect the predicted evolutionary trajectories.
claims.source: First, the analysis was repeated using scores for presence or absence of traits that were assigned by hierarchical clustering, as opposed to using the EM algorithm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). Although hierarchical clustering generated differences in the scoring of a small number of traits, the predicted evolutionary trajectories were not affected, producing highly similar results (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This robustness test is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Removing two independent pairs of traits from the analysis did not affect the predicted timing of the remaining 14 traits.
claims.source: Removing two independent pairs of traits from the analysis did not affect the predicted timing of the remaining 14 traits (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This robustness test is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B.

claims.claim: Including two additional traits associated with C4 photosynthesis did not alter the predicted timing of other traits.
claims.source: Furthermore, including two additional traits associated with C4 photosynthesis also did not alter the predicted timing of other traits (C).
claims.evidence: This robustness test is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: The centripetal positioning of mitochondria and the centrifugal or centripetal position of chloroplasts within BS cells are predicted to be acquired early in the evolution of C4 photosynthesis.
claims.source: Consistent with observations made from several genera, we predict that these cellular alterations are acquired early in the evolution of C4 photosynthesis (Hylton et al., 1988; McKown and Dengler, 2007; Muhaidat et al., 2011; Sage et al., 2011b).
claims.evidence: This prediction is consistent with cited observations from multiple genera.

claims.claim: Inflexible linkage between multiple traits was detected in artificial positive control datasets but not in the C3–C4 dataset.
claims.source: Inflexible linkage between multiple traits was detected in artificial positive control datasets (Figure 2B) but not in the C3–C4 dataset (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing results from positive controls (Figure 2B) with the biological data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claims.claim: The order of C4 trait acquisition is flexible.
claims.source: This result suggests that the order of C4 trait acquisition is flexible.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the contingency analysis showing no inflexible linkage between traits.

claims.claim: Multiple origins of C4 may have been facilitated by flexibility in the evolutionary pathways connecting C3 and C4 phenotypes.
claims.source: Multiple origins of C4 may therefore have been facilitated by this flexibility in the evolutionary pathways connecting C3 and C4 phenotypes.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the finding of flexible trait acquisition order.

claims.claim: No single sequence of acquisitions was capable of producing intermediate phenotypes compatible with all observations.
claims.source: First, no single sequence of acquisitions was capable of producing intermediate phenotypes compatible with all observations ('Methods').
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from the dynamic programming analysis described in Methods.

claims.claim: Several traits such as compartmentation of GDC into BS and the increased number of chloroplasts in the BS displayed bimodal probability distributions for their acquisition.
claims.source: Second, several traits such as compartmentation of GDC into BS and the increased number of chloroplasts in the BS clearly displayed bimodal probability distributions for their acquisition (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the probability distributions in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Bimodality in acquisition probabilities is indicative of multiple distinct pathways to C4 photosynthesis that acquire traits at earlier or later times.
claims.source: This bimodality is indicative of multiple distinct pathways to C4 photosynthesis that acquire traits at earlier or later times.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the bimodal distributions observed in the data.

claims.claim: PCA on the entire set of inferred transition networks for monocot and dicot subsets revealed distinct separation.
claims.source: PCA on the entire set of inferred transition networks for monocot and dicot subsets revealed distinct separation (Figure 4A)
claims.evidence: This is shown in the PCA plot in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The topology of the evolutionary landscape surrounding C4 is largely different for monocots and eudicots.
claims.source: PCA on the entire set of inferred transition networks for monocot and dicot subsets revealed distinct separation (Figure 4A), suggesting that the topology of the evolutionary landscape surrounding C4 is largely different for these two anciently diverged taxa.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the PCA results shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The separation between monocot and eudicot evolutionary landscapes is the result of differences in the timing of events generating both anatomical and biochemical traits.
claims.source: Analysis of the posterior probabilities of the mean pathways representing either monocots or dicots revealed that this separation is the result of differences in the timing of events generating both anatomical and biochemical traits (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the analysis presented in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The ancient divergence of the monocot and eudicot clades constrained the evolution of C4 photosynthesis to broadly different evolutionary pathways in each.
claims.source: We propose that the ancient divergence of the monocot and eudicot clades constrained the evolution of C4 photosynthesis to broadly different evolutionary pathways in each.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed differences between monocot and eudicot pathways.

claims.claim: There was more overlap between the landscapes generating NAD–ME and NADP-ME species than between monocots and eudicots.
claims.source: There was more overlap between the landscapes generating NAD–ME and NADP-ME species (Figure 4B), likely reflecting the convergent origins of NAD–ME and NADP-ME sub-types (Furbank, 2011; Sage et al., 2011a).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the PCA plot in Figure 4B and interpreted with reference to cited literature.

claims.claim: In NAD–ME lineages, increased vein density was predicted to be acquired early in C4 evolution, while in NADP-ME species this trait showed a broadly different trajectory.
claims.source: For example, in NAD–ME lineages, increased vein density was predicted to be acquired early in C4 evolution, while in NADP-ME species this trait showed a broadly different trajectory (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the analysis presented in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The proliferation of chloroplasts in the BS was acquired with different timings between the NAD-ME and NADP-ME sub-types.
claims.source: The proliferation of chloroplasts in the BS was also acquired with different timings between the two sub-types.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of NAD-ME and NADP-ME lineages.

claims.claim: The alternative evolutionary pathways generating the NADP-ME and NAD–ME subtypes were defined by differences in the timing of anatomical and cellular traits that precede the majority of biochemical alterations.
claims.source: The alternative evolutionary pathways generating the NADP-ME and NAD–ME subtypes were therefore defined by differences in the timing of anatomical and cellular traits that are predicted to precede the majority of biochemical alterations (Figure 3, Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis shown in Figures 3 and 4D.

claims.claim: Distinct C4 sub-types evolved as a consequence of alternative evolutionary histories in response to non-photosynthetic pressures.
claims.source: We therefore conclude that these distinct sub-types evolved as a consequence of alternative evolutionary histories in response to non-photosynthetic pressures.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that anatomical differences precede biochemical differences between subtypes.

claims.claim: Early evolutionary events determined the downstream phenotypes of C4 sub-types by restricting lineages to independent pathways across phenotype space.
claims.source: Furthermore, we propose that early evolutionary events determined the downstream phenotypes of C4 sub-types by restricting lineages to independent pathways across phenotype space.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the evolution of different C4 subtypes.

claims.claim: The novel Bayesian approach is not dependent on detailed phylogenetic inference.
claims.source: However, as our approach is not dependent on detailed phylogenetic inference, we propose that it could be used to model the evolution of other complex traits, such as those in the fossil record, which are also currently limited by the fragmented nature of data available (Kidwell and Holland, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a property of the developed method.

claims.claim: The approach could be used to model the evolution of other complex traits in the fossil record.
claims.source: However, as our approach is not dependent on detailed phylogenetic inference, we propose that it could be used to model the evolution of other complex traits, such as those in the fossil record, which are also currently limited by the fragmented nature of data available (Kidwell and Holland, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed application of the method with citation to relevant literature.

claims.claim: The approach may be useful in inferring pathways underlying stochastic processes occurring over shorter timescales, such as disease or tumour progression, or cell type differentiation.
claims.source: Our approach is also not limited by the time-scale over which predicted trajectories occur. As a result, it may be useful in inferring pathways underlying stochastic processes occurring over much shorter timescales, such as disease or tumour progression, or the differentiation of cell types.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed application of the method.

claims.claim: According to the hypothesis that declining CO2 drove C4 evolution, alterations to PEPC and RuBisCO would be expected to occur early in the evolutionary trajectories generating C4.
claims.source: A central hypothesis for the ecological drivers of C4 evolution is that declining CO2 concentration in the Oligocene decreased the rate of carboxylation by RuBisCO, creating a strong pressure to evolve alternative photosynthetic strategies (Christin et al., 2008; Vicentini et al., 2008). According to this hypothesis, alterations to the localisation and abundance of the primary carboxylases PEPC and RuBisCO would be expected to occur early in the evolutionary trajectories generating C4.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the cited hypothesis about CO2-driven evolution.

claims.claim: The data suggest that alterations to anatomy and cell biology preceded the majority of biochemical alterations, contrary to the CO2-driven hypothesis.
claims.source: Conversely, our data suggest that alterations to anatomy and cell biology were predicted to precede the majority of biochemical alterations, and that other enzymes of the C4 pathway are recruited prior to PEPC and RuBisCO (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 3 that contradicts the CO2-driven hypothesis.

claims.claim: Enzymes such as PPDK and C4 acid decarboxylases function in processes not related to photosynthesis within leaves of C3 plants.
claims.source: These enzymes, such as PPDK and C4 acid decarboxylases, function in processes not related to photosynthesis within leaves of C3 plants (Aubry et al., 2011)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Aubry et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The early changes to abundance and localisation of PPDK and C4 acid decarboxylases within C4 lineages may have been driven by non-photosynthetic pressures.
claims.source: These enzymes, such as PPDK and C4 acid decarboxylases, function in processes not related to photosynthesis within leaves of C3 plants (Aubry et al., 2011), so the early changes to abundance and localisation of these enzymes within C4 lineages may have been driven by non-photosynthetic pressures.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on the finding that these enzymes are recruited early and have non-photosynthetic functions.

claims.claim: A recent in silico study predicts that changes to photorespiratory metabolism and GDC in BS cells evolved prior to the C4 pathway.
claims.source: A recent in silico study also predicts that changes to photorespiratory metabolism and GDC in BS cells evolved prior to the C4 pathway (Heckman et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Heckman et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The model predicts that BS-specificity of GDC was acquired early in C4 evolution for the majority of lineages.
claims.source: Our model predicts that BS-specificity of GDC was acquired early in C4 evolution for the majority of lineages.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model.

claims.claim: The predicted timing of GDC BS-specificity is bimodal and not predicted to be acquired early in monocot lineages.
claims.source: However, we also note that the predicted timing of GDC BS-specificity is bimodal in our analysis (Figure 3), and not predicted to be acquired early in monocot lineages (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the analysis presented in Figures 3 and 4C.

claims.claim: BS-specificity of GDC is not a feature of C4 evolution to have occurred repeatedly in all lineages.
claims.source: These results suggest that this is not a feature of C4 evolution to have occurred repeatedly in all lineages.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bimodal distribution and differences between monocots and eudicots.

claims.claim: Recent evidence has identified additional environmental pressures that may have driven C4 evolution, including high evaporative demands and increased fire frequency.
claims.source: Recent evidence from physiological and ecological studies has identified a number of additional environmental pressures that may have driven the evolution and radiation of C4 lineages, including high evaporative demands (Osborne and Sack, 2012) and increased fire frequency (Edwards et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies.

claims.claim: Increased BS volume and vein density have been proposed as likely adaptations to improve leaf hydraulics under drought.
claims.source: Increased BS volume and vein density have been proposed as likely adaptations to improve leaf hydraulics under drought (Osborne and Sack, 2012; Griffiths et al. 2013)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies.

claims.claim: Differences in the timing of events altering leaf vascular development and BS chloroplast division occur prior to the appearance of the alternative evolutionary pathways generating the NADP-ME and NAD-ME biochemical sub-types.
claims.source: For example, we find that differences in the timing of events altering leaf vascular development and BS chloroplast division occur prior to the appearance of the alternative evolutionary pathways generating the NADP-ME and NAD-ME biochemical sub-types (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the analysis presented in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: These anatomical and cellular traits are predicted to evolve prior to any alterations to the C4 acid decarboxylase enzymes that traditionally define the NADP-ME and NAD-ME sub-types.
claims.source: These traits are predicted to evolve prior to any alterations to the C4 acid decarboxylase enzymes that traditionally define these sub-types (Furbank, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model with reference to the traditional classification.

claims.claim: An homologous mechanism has been shown to regulate the cell-specificity of gene expression in both NADP-ME and NAD-ME gene families in independent lineages.
claims.source: As an homologous mechanism has been shown to regulate the cell-specificity of gene expression in both NADP-ME and NAD-ME gene families in independent lineages (Brown et al., 2011)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2011.

claims.claim: It is unlikely that mechanisms underlying the recruitment of decarboxylase enzymes drove the evolution of distinct C4 sub-types.
claims.source: As an homologous mechanism has been shown to regulate the cell-specificity of gene expression in both NADP-ME and NAD-ME gene families in independent lineages (Brown et al., 2011), it is unlikely that mechanisms underlying the recruitment of these enzymes drove the evolution of distinct sub-types.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the finding of homologous mechanisms and the timing of trait acquisition.

claims.claim: Different C4 sub-types evolved as a consequence of alternative evolutionary histories in leaf development, rather than biochemical or photosynthetic pressures.
claims.source: We therefore conclude that these different sub-types evolved as a consequence of alternative evolutionary histories in leaf development, rather than biochemical or photosynthetic pressures.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that anatomical differences precede biochemical differences.

claims.claim: Differences in the carboxylation efficiency or photosynthetic performance of different C4 sub-types have never been detected.
claims.source: This may explain why differences in the carboxylation efficiency or photosynthetic performance of different C4 sub-types have never been detected (Furbank, 2011), making the adaptive significance of different decarboxylation mechanisms difficult to explain.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Furbank, 2011.

claims.claim: At least four distinct evolutionary trajectories underlie the evolution of C4 lineages.
claims.source: First, we show that at least four distinct evolutionary trajectories underlie the evolution of C4 lineages (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the comparative analysis presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: There is no evidence for inflexible linkage between the predicted timing of distinct C4 traits.
claims.source: Second, we find no evidence for inflexible linkage between the predicted timing of distinct C4 traits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the contingency analysis presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 (note: the text says supplement 1 but likely refers to supplement 3).

claims.claim: Diversity in viable pathways helps explain why C4 has been accessible to such a wide variety of species.
claims.source: This diversity in viable pathways also helps explain why C4 has been accessible to such a wide variety of species and not limited to a smaller subset of the angiosperm phylogeny.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the finding of multiple flexible pathways.

claims.claim: A recent model for the evolution of C4 biochemistry found that C4 photosynthesis was accessible from any surrounding point of a fitness landscape.
claims.source: A recent model for the evolution of the biochemistry associated with the C4 leaf also found that C4 photosynthesis was accessible from any surrounding point of a fitness landscape (Heckman et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Heckman et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The trajectories predicted by Heckman et al. (2013) were found to pass through phenotypes of C3–C4 species, despite these species not being used to parameterise the evolutionary landscape.
claims.source: Encouragingly, the trajectories predicted by Heckman et al. (2013) were found to pass through phenotypes of C3–C4 species, despite the fact that these species were not used to parameterise the evolutionary landscape.
claims.evidence: This statement describes a finding from Heckman et al., 2013 that supports the current study's conclusions.

claims.claim: Different mechanisms generate increased abundance and cell-specificity for the majority of C4 enzymes in independent C4 lineages.
claims.source: As different mechanisms generate increased abundance and cell-specificity for the majority C4 enzymes in independent C4 lineages (reviewed in Langdale, 2011; Williams et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claims.claim: Mechanistic diversity likely underlies the multiple evolutionary pathways generating C4 photosynthesis and may be a key factor in facilitating the convergent evolution of complex traits.
claims.source: As different mechanisms generate increased abundance and cell-specificity for the majority C4 enzymes in independent C4 lineages (reviewed in Langdale, 2011; Williams et al., 2012), it is likely that mechanistic diversity underlies the multiple evolutionary pathways generating C4 photosynthesis and may be a key factor in facilitating the convergent evolution of complex traits.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed explanation linking mechanistic diversity to pathway flexibility.

claims.claim: The flexibility in evolutionary pathways may benefit efforts to recapitulate C4 photosynthesis through genetic engineering of C3 species.
claims.source: This may benefit efforts to recapitulate the acquisition of C4 photosynthesis through the genetic engineering of C3 species (Hibberd et al., 2008), expanding the molecular toolbox available to establish C4 traits in distinct phenotypic backgrounds.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed application of the findings with citation to relevant engineering efforts.

results.result: A meta-analysis was conducted consolidating data from 43 studies encompassing 18 C3, 18 C4, and 37 C3–C4 intermediate species from 22 genera representing 18 independent lineages. The data were used to parameterize a 16-dimensional phenotypic landscape with 65,536 nodes, with quantitative traits assigned binary scores using EM algorithm and hierarchical clustering. PCA confirmed the phenotypic intermediacy of C3–C4 species between C3 and C4 phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C18-C20, C22-C27 collectively describe the meta-analysis methodology and data structure. The dataset composition is clearly documented in Table 1, the binary scoring methodology is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and PCA results confirming intermediacy are shown in Figure 1A. The mathematical structure of the phenotype space (2^16 = 65,536 nodes) is correctly calculated and the phylogenetic relationships are supported by citations.

results.result: A novel Bayesian approach based on Hidden Markov Models was developed to model the phenotypic landscape as a transition network with weighted edges. The approach uses Bayesian MCMC to sample networks compatible with the meta-analysis dataset, imposing constraints that only one trait may be acquired at a time and trait loss is forbidden.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C28-C31 describe the novel computational methodology. The HMM framework is properly cited (Rabiner, 1989), the transition network structure is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and the Methods section provides detailed mathematical formulation including the MCMC sampling procedure. The constraints are explicitly stated and justified as modeling assumptions.

results.result: The Bayesian approach was validated using artificial datasets and experimental verification. The method correctly assigned equal acquisition probabilities to traits with linked timing even with 50% data occlusion, correctly predicted 15 of 18 strongly predicted traits from occluded biological data, and predictions were experimentally verified by qPCR for enzyme abundance.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 describe validation results shown in Figure 2. The positive control tests (Figure 2A-B) demonstrate the method can detect simultaneous trait acquisition. The cross-validation with occluded data (Figure 2C) shows high accuracy (15/18 correct strong predictions, 83% accuracy). The qPCR experimental validation (Figure 2D-E) provides independent confirmation of model predictions. The conservative nature of predictions (11 neutral vs. 3 incorrect) supports reliability.

results.result: The model predicts that alterations to leaf anatomy, cell-specificity, and increased abundance of C4 cycle enzymes evolved prior to alterations in RuBisCO and PEPC. BS cell enlargement was predicted as an early innovation, BS-specificity of GDC occurs early, and RuBisCO loss from M cells occurs late. For most C4 enzymes except PEPC, increased abundance and cellular compartmentation were temporally separated.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C43 describe the main evolutionary trajectory findings shown in Figure 3. The temporal ordering is clearly depicted with posterior probability distributions. The findings are consistent with previous studies (properly cited: Hylton et al., 1988; Rawsthorne et al., 1988; Cheng et al., 1988; Khoshravesh et al., 2012) and with molecular studies showing different cis-elements mediate abundance vs. specificity (Akyildiz et al., 2007; Kajala et al., 2012). The separation of abundance and compartmentation for non-PEPC enzymes is a novel finding supported by the data.

results.result: Robustness analyses demonstrated that the predicted evolutionary trajectories were not affected by using hierarchical clustering instead of EM algorithm for trait scoring, removing two independent pairs of traits, or adding two additional cellular traits (mitochondria and chloroplast positioning).
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 describe robustness tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1-2. The comparison between EM and hierarchical clustering (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) shows highly similar results despite differences in trait scoring. The trait removal tests (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B) and trait addition test (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) demonstrate that conclusions are robust to changes in the phenotype space structure. These sensitivity analyses strengthen confidence in the main findings.

results.result: The order of C4 trait acquisition is flexible, with no inflexible linkage detected between traits in the biological data (unlike positive controls). No single sequence of acquisitions was compatible with all observations, and several traits displayed bimodal probability distributions, indicating multiple distinct pathways to C4 photosynthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 describe the flexibility analysis. The contingency analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) shows no inflexible linkage in biological data, contrasting with positive controls (Figure 2B) where linkage was successfully detected. The bimodal distributions for traits like GDC compartmentation and BS chloroplast number (Figure 3) provide direct evidence for multiple pathways. The dynamic programming analysis confirming no single pathway fits all data is stated in Methods. These multiple lines of evidence converge on pathway flexibility.

results.result: At least four distinct evolutionary trajectories underlie C4 evolution, with monocot and eudicot lineages showing distinct separation in PCA of inferred transition networks. The separation results from differences in timing of both anatomical and biochemical trait acquisition, suggesting ancestral lineage constrains evolutionary pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57, C83 describe the identification of multiple trajectories shown in Figure 4. The PCA separation between monocots and eudicots (Figure 4A) is clear and robust (confirmed in Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The timing differences are shown in Figure 4C. However, C57 is labeled as speculation in the evidence, and the causal claim that 'ancient divergence constrained' evolution is an inference rather than directly demonstrated. The four trajectories (monocot/eudicot × NADP-ME/NAD-ME) are supported by the comparative analyses.

results.result: NAD-ME and NADP-ME subtypes show more overlap than monocot/eudicot comparisons but differ in timing of anatomical traits. Vein density increases early in NAD-ME but not NADP-ME lineages, and BS chloroplast proliferation timing differs between subtypes. These anatomical differences precede biochemical alterations to decarboxylase enzymes that traditionally define the subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61, C77-C78 describe subtype-specific trajectories shown in Figure 4B and 4D. The PCA shows more overlap between NAD-ME and NADP-ME than between monocots and eudicots (Figure 4A vs 4B), consistent with convergent origins. The timing differences for vein density and chloroplast proliferation are clearly shown in Figure 4D. The finding that anatomical differences precede biochemical differences is a key result supported by the temporal ordering in the model.

results.result: Distinct C4 sub-types evolved as a consequence of alternative evolutionary histories in response to non-photosynthetic pressures rather than biochemical or photosynthetic pressures. Early evolutionary events determined downstream phenotypes by restricting lineages to independent pathways, and homologous mechanisms for decarboxylase recruitment make it unlikely these enzymes drove subtype evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63, C80-C81 present interpretations and conclusions about the drivers of subtype evolution. While the finding that anatomical changes precede biochemical changes is well-supported (C61, C77-C78), the causal claims about 'non-photosynthetic pressures' driving evolution (C62, C81) are inferences not directly tested. The argument about homologous mechanisms (C80, citing Brown et al., 2011) is logical but indirect. The claim that early events 'determined' downstream phenotypes (C63) is speculative. These are reasonable interpretations but lack direct experimental evidence for the proposed causal mechanisms.

results.result: The data contradict the CO2-driven hypothesis for C4 evolution, which predicts early alterations to PEPC and RuBisCO. Instead, anatomical and cellular changes preceded biochemical alterations, and enzymes like PPDK and decarboxylases (which have non-photosynthetic functions in C3 plants) were recruited early, suggesting non-photosynthetic drivers.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 present an argument against the prevailing CO2-driven hypothesis. The CO2 hypothesis and its predictions are properly cited (Christin et al., 2008; Vicentini et al., 2008). The model results (Figure 3) clearly show anatomical changes precede PEPC and RuBisCO alterations, contradicting the hypothesis. The observation that early-recruited enzymes have non-photosynthetic functions in C3 plants (C69, citing Aubry et al., 2011) is factual. However, the inference that this indicates non-photosynthetic drivers (C70) is speculative, though reasonable given the evidence.

results.result: The model predicts BS-specificity of GDC was acquired early in C4 evolution for most lineages, consistent with a recent in silico study. However, the timing is bimodal and not predicted to be early in monocot lineages, suggesting this is not a universal feature across all C4 lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 describe GDC evolution findings. The consistency with Heckman et al. (2013) is properly cited (C71). The bimodal distribution for GDC timing is visible in Figure 3 (C73), and the monocot-specific pattern is shown in Figure 4C. The conclusion that GDC BS-specificity is not universal (C74) follows logically from the bimodal distribution and lineage-specific differences. This nuanced finding adds complexity to previous models suggesting universal early GDC recruitment.

results.result: Recent evidence has identified additional environmental pressures beyond CO2 that may have driven C4 evolution, including high evaporative demands and increased fire frequency. Increased BS volume and vein density have been proposed as adaptations to improve leaf hydraulics under drought.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 cite recent literature on alternative ecological drivers (Osborne and Sack, 2012; Edwards et al., 2010; Griffiths et al., 2013). These are properly attributed to prior work and provide context for interpreting the finding that anatomical changes precede biochemical changes. The claims accurately represent the cited literature.

results.result: Differences in carboxylation efficiency between C4 sub-types have never been detected, making adaptive significance of different decarboxylation mechanisms difficult to explain. The diversity in viable pathways helps explain C4 accessibility across diverse species. Mechanistic diversity in enzyme regulation likely underlies multiple evolutionary pathways and facilitates convergent evolution of complex traits.
results.evaluation: Claims C82, C85-C89 synthesize findings with literature. The lack of performance differences between subtypes (C82) is properly cited (Furbank, 2011) and helps explain why anatomical rather than biochemical differences distinguish subtypes. The connection between pathway diversity and C4 accessibility (C85) is a logical inference from the flexibility findings. The consistency with Heckman et al. (2013) model (C86-C87) provides independent support. The link between mechanistic diversity and pathway flexibility (C88-C89) is reasonable but somewhat speculative, though supported by citations to reviews (Langdale, 2011; Williams et al., 2012).

results.result: The novel Bayesian approach is not dependent on detailed phylogenetic inference and could be applied to model evolution of other complex traits in the fossil record or stochastic processes over shorter timescales such as disease progression or cell differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 describe potential applications of the method. The independence from phylogenetic inference (C64) is a stated property of the method and is evident from the modeling approach which uses phenotypic data rather than phylogenetic trees. The proposed applications to fossil record (C65, citing Kidwell and Holland, 2002) and shorter timescale processes (C66) are reasonable extrapolations given the method's properties, though these remain untested hypotheses. These are appropriate forward-looking statements about method applicability.

results.result: The flexibility in evolutionary pathways may benefit efforts to engineer C4 photosynthesis into C3 species by expanding the molecular toolbox available to establish C4 traits in distinct phenotypic backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Claim C90 proposes an application to C4 engineering efforts (citing Hibberd et al., 2008). This is a reasonable inference from the pathway flexibility findings—if multiple routes to C4 exist in nature, engineering efforts need not follow a single prescribed path. However, this remains a speculative application that would require experimental validation. The claim is appropriately framed as a potential benefit rather than a demonstrated outcome.

results.result: Background claims establish that C4 photosynthesis evolved independently in at least 60 lineages starting 32-25 million years ago in response to ecological drivers including decreasing CO2. C4 plants have modified Kranz anatomy with compartmentalized metabolism between mesophyll and bundle sheath cells, with three biochemical subtypes based on decarboxylase enzymes. C3-C4 intermediates represent evolutionary transitional states.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C17, C21 provide established background knowledge properly cited to the literature (Sage et al., 2011a; Christin et al., 2011b; Vicentini et al., 2008; Slack and Hatch, 1967; Langdale, 2011; Hattersley, 1984; Hatch et al., 1975; Furbank, 2011; Akyildiz et al., 2007; Brown et al., 2011; and others). These claims accurately represent the current understanding of C4 photosynthesis and provide necessary context for the study. The characterization of C3-C4 intermediates as transitional states (C21) is supported by phylogenetic evidence from multiple cited studies.

results.result: The polyphyletic appearance of C4 photosynthesis is associated with diverse and flexible evolutionary paths grouping into four major trajectories. Alternative evolutionary histories were determined by ancestral lineage and initial phenotypic alterations unrelated to photosynthesis. The order of trait acquisition is flexible and driven by non-photosynthetic drivers, and this flexibility facilitated convergent evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C5-C7 represent the main conclusions of the study. The four trajectories (C2) are supported by the monocot/eudicot and NADP-ME/NAD-ME analyses (Figure 4). The role of ancestral lineage (C5) is demonstrated by the monocot/eudicot differences (Figure 4A, C). The flexibility in trait acquisition order (C6) is supported by the contingency analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and absence of inflexible linkage. The claim about non-photosynthetic drivers (C6) is supported by the finding that anatomical changes precede biochemical changes (Figure 3). The inference that flexibility facilitated convergence (C7) is logical given the multiple pathways identified.
